metrics.title: What the AI-first model buys you

items.label: Cost
items.detail: The same senior team, but you are not billed hours for the frame a machine can type.

items.label: Speed
items.detail: Form-heavy sites come in close to twice as fast. Research-heavy work less so. Discovery on Monday, a running version by the end of the sprint.

items.label: Interface
items.detail: A designer joins the first call. You approve the screens before we write what sits behind them.

items.label: Ownership
items.detail: Source code, servers and accounts are all in your name. Drop us whenever you like and another team can pick it straight up.

metrics.footnote: The speed figure compares the same scope against the traditional way of building it. We show you the arithmetic during discovery.

aiFirst.title: What AI actually does on your project
aiFirst.subtitle: Plainly: the machine does the repetitive part, people do the part that goes wrong.

items.title: The machine types the frame, people decide the hard parts
items.body: Repetitive code gets generated in minutes. How it is built, how it is secured and where it is likely to break stay with senior engineers. Those are the parts that cost you money when they are wrong.

items.title: The machine checks first, people check after
items.body: Every code change runs through automated checks: syntax errors, security holes, outdated libraries. Human review starts where the machine stopped.

items.title: Change a requirement and you see what breaks
items.body: Your requirements are written as automated checks sitting next to the code. Change one thing and the system tells you what it drags along, instead of surfacing three weeks later.

items.title: We can put AI in your product too
items.body: A chatbot that answers from your own documents, automatic sorting of orders, summarised feedback. We run these in our own products first, so you skip the tuition.

items.q: Can I edit the content myself afterwards?
items.a: Yes. There is an admin area where you change text, swap images and add posts. Handover includes a training session, recorded so you can rewatch it later.

items.q: How soon do I see what it looks like?
items.a: Within the first week or two you are approving the interface in Figma and clicking through it like the real thing. Changes at that point are cheap because no code exists yet.

items.q: What if I have no content or photos?
items.a: Normal, most clients do not. We build with correctly structured placeholder content and hand you a checklist of what to prepare. We can introduce a photographer and a copywriter if you want.

items.q: If it costs less, is it worse?
items.a: The savings are hours nobody has to type, not people cut or reviews skipped. Senior engineers still read every line. Ask us to open a real pull request during discovery and pick it apart.

items.q: Will the site rank on Google by itself?
items.a: Not by itself. We build it so Google can read it, load it fast and find the sitemap. Ranking then needs steady content and time. Anyone promising page one immediately is guessing.

items.q: What if I am not happy with it?
items.a: Every stage has an approval gate, so nothing runs to the end before a mismatch surfaces. Design keeps iterating until you approve it, and only then do we write code.

items.q: Who looks after it once the warranty ends?
items.a: There is an optional annual maintenance plan covering infrastructure, security patches, backups and support. If you skip it, the source code is yours and another team can take over.
You do, from the first commit. We work in your repository and your cloud accounts. There is no platform of ours you have to keep paying for.
